question: Q1: Which L2 regularization strength (lambda) minimizes 5-fold CV Brier score for logistic regression?
rationale: Standard L2 regularization practice for classification: weak regularization often improves generalization by penalizing large weights. Cross-validation estimates true generalization error on unseen data. Brier score is proper scoring rule for probabilistic predictions.
decision: Test all 5 lambda values via 5-fold contiguous block CV using exact full-batch GD optimizer (200 iters, lr=0.1). Select lambda with lowest mean Brier score. Report improvement vs baseline (lambda=0).
expected_effect: Expect moderate lambda (0.01-0.1) to perform best, with improvement over baseline of 0.01-0.05 Brier points depending on feature scale and sample size. Extreme lambdas (0, 10.0) likely perform worse due to underfitting or overfitting respectively.
falsifier: If lowest CV Brier is not among [lambda=0.0, 0.01, 0.1, 1.0, 10.0], or if all lambdas yield identical Brier score (within floating point tolerance), the test is inconclusive and should report which lambda was best within the tested set.

question: Q2: Do interaction features (x0*x1, x1*x2, x2*x3, x0*x3) significantly improve logistic regression with lambda=0.1?
alternatives: Do not add interactions, report t-stat as 0
Add interactions and test if t > 2.0 threshold
Add interactions but use different test (e.g., Wilcoxon)
rationale: Paired t-test is standard for comparing two correlated samples (same 5 folds). Threshold t > 2.0 is conventional (roughly p < 0.05 for df=4). Interaction features may capture nonlinear relationships; test empirically on this dataset.
decision: Fit logistic regression with lambda=0.1 on raw features and again on raw+interaction features using 5-fold CV. For each fold, compute Brier scores. Run paired t-test: t = mean(fold_brier_raw - fold_brier_interaction) / (std / sqrt(5)). Set interaction_helps=true if t > 2.0.
expected_effect: If interactions capture real structure, raw Brier should be higher (worse) than interaction Brier, yielding t > 2.0. If interactions are spurious, t-stat will be near 0 or negative.
falsifier: If paired t-test calculation is undefined (e.g., all fold differences = 0), report t-stat as computed value and interaction_helps according to the t > 2.0 rule applied to whatever t is obtained.

question: Q3: Which compression configuration (sparsity %, quantization bits) retains the most dense model performance?
rationale: Model compression trades off model size vs. accuracy. Retention = dense_brier / compressed_brier measures this tradeoff. Highest retention means the compressed model is closest to dense model performance. Test all 6 configs systematically.
decision: Fit dense logistic model on all training data with lambda=0.1 using full-batch GD. Compute in-sample Brier (dense baseline). For each of 6 configs: apply sparsity (zero smallest |w|), then quantize remaining weights uniformly to 2^bits levels. Compute in-sample Brier on compressed model. Retention = dense_brier / compressed_brier. Report config with highest retention as string 'sparsityXX_bitsY'.
expected_effect: Expect moderate sparsity (20-40%) with higher bits (8) to perform best. Extreme sparsity (60%) likely to reduce retention significantly. 4-bit quantization adds noise but may be acceptable with lower sparsity.
falsifier: If all configs yield same retention (floating point), report which config was tested first. If retention > 1.0 (compressed brier < dense brier), verify calculation and report as computed (indicates noise reduction from compression).
